title: Metrics Monitoring and Alerting (Prometheus-style)
problem: Design a metrics monitoring and alerting system for a fleet of ~10,000 servers and thousands of services, Prometheus/Grafana-style.
summary: A pull-based metrics pipeline: instrumented apps expose /metrics, a collector scrapes them on a fixed interval, samples land in a time-series DB (TSDB) with delta-of-delta + XOR float compression, an alert engine continuously evaluates PromQL-style rules, and Grafana queries the TSDB for dashboards. The dominant design choice is pull-based scraping over push: pull makes service-discovery the source of truth for the target list, and a target failing to be scraped is itself a signal (up==0). The main tradeoff is short-lived batch jobs, which can finish before a scrape — those go through an optional push gateway. Sized for ~10M active series and ~1M samples/sec ingest, which fits Prometheus on a handful of nodes and spills to a remote long-term TSDB (Thanos / Mimir / VictoriaMetrics) for retention beyond 15 days.

functional: Collect counter, gauge, histogram, and summary metrics from ~10,000 hosts and thousands of services
Expose a /metrics endpoint per process in Prometheus text exposition format
Scrape all targets on a configurable interval (typically 15 or 30 seconds)
Store samples for at least 15 days locally and 12 months in a remote long-term TSDB
Evaluate PromQL-style alerting rules continuously and dispatch notifications
Serve ad-hoc queries from Grafana with sub-second latency on the last hour of data
nonFunctional: Ingest at least 1 million samples per second per collector
Support 10 million active series per collector without OOM
Scrape failures must themselves be observable (up == 0 is the signal)
Alerting latency under 60 seconds from threshold breach to notification
Graceful degradation: if the remote TSDB is down, local retention continues
Instrumentation overhead under 1% CPU and negligible allocation on the hot path

assumptions: 10K hosts * ~1000 active series each = ~10M active series
Scrape interval: 15s default; alert eval interval: 30s
Sample size on disk: ~1.3 bytes/sample (Gorilla / Facebook compression)
Retention: 15 days hot local TSDB, 13 months remote long-term storage
estimates: Hot storage: 57.6B * 1.3B * 15d ≈ 1.1 TB across the TSDB cluster
Query load: Grafana ~500 concurrent dashboards * 6 panels each ≈ 3K PromQL/sec peak
Alert eval: 2000 rules / 30s ≈ 67 evals/sec, each touching a handful of series

architecture.mermaid: graph LR app[Instrumented App] --> collector[Scrape Collector] pushgw[Push Gateway] --> collector collector --> kafka[Metrics Kafka] kafka --> tsdb[(Time Series DB)] tsdb --> alertengine[Alert Rule Engine] tsdb --> grafana[Grafana] alertengine --> notifier[Notification Sender] grafana --> client[Operator Browser]

client.name: Operator Browser
client.summary: SRE/developer browser rendering Grafana dashboards and receiving pager notifications.

sections.heading: Responsibilities
sections.body:
- Open Grafana dashboards; Grafana fans out PromQL queries to the TSDB
- Receive PagerDuty / Slack notifications from the alert notifier
- Acknowledge / silence alerts via Alertmanager UI

sections.heading: Latency expectations
sections.body:
- Dashboard panel load: < 2s p95 for a 1h range
- Alert delivery: < 1 min from condition-true to pager

sections.heading: Why this matters for beginners
sections.body: Monitoring is read-heavy from humans but write-heavy from infrastructure. Dashboards and alerts are two very different query shapes against the same TSDB.

bottlenecks.title: Dashboard panel fan-out overwhelms browser
bottlenecks.trigger: Operator opens a dense dashboard with 20+ panels; each panel fires its own PromQL query_range. With the design's 500 concurrent dashboards × 6 panels = 3K PromQL/sec peak, a single power-user dashboard can issue 20+ parallel XHRs hitting the browser's per-origin connection cap (~6 in HTTP/1.1).
bottlenecks.symptom: Dashboard takes 10–30s to fully render; panels load in visible waves; browser tab pegs a CPU core; p95 panel load blows past the 2s target.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable Grafana's HTTP/2 to the data source, turn on query result caching (Grafana Enterprise query cache or a Trickster/nginx cache in front of the TSDB), lower panel count per dashboard (<12), and use `$__interval` so step scales with range instead of returning 1000s of points per panel.
bottlenecks.detection: Track Grafana's `grafana_http_request_duration_seconds` p95 per dashboard UID, browser RUM `first-contentful-paint` and long-task counts, and alert when panel query p95 > 2s for more than 5 minutes.

bottlenecks.title: High-cardinality template variable dropdowns
bottlenecks.trigger: Dashboard load issues `label_values(instance)` against the 10M-active-series TSDB; with 10K hosts the dropdown returns 10K+ entries and the query scans the full label index.
bottlenecks.symptom: Dashboard is blank for 3–8s on first load while variable dropdowns resolve; `$instance` dropdown is sluggish or truncated; occasional 504s from Grafana when the label query exceeds timeout.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Scope variable queries with a job filter (`label_values(up{job="api"}, instance)`), cap results via Grafana's variable `regex` filter, cache label values on the TSDB side (Prometheus `--query.max-samples` tuning / Mimir label cache), and avoid variables on labels with >1K distinct values.
bottlenecks.detection: Log and alert on `/api/v1/label/*/values` queries with latency > 1s or result size > 5000; track Grafana variable-refresh time from browser RUM.

bottlenecks.title: Alert notification latency exceeds 1 min SLO
bottlenecks.trigger: End-to-end delivery budget is <1 min, but the pipeline already spends 30s on alert eval granularity + gossip-based HA Alertmanager dedup (1–2s) + provider webhook retry/backoff. If PagerDuty or Slack has a transient outage, exponential backoff pushes delivery beyond the SLO.
bottlenecks.symptom: On-call pager fires 90s+ after condition crossed `for:` duration; Slack message arrives minutes after PagerDuty; occasional missed pages during provider incidents.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Reduce alert eval interval from 30s to 15s for `severity=page` rules, configure multiple redundant receivers (PagerDuty primary + email/SMS fallback), set `group_wait: 0s` for critical routes, and monitor Alertmanager's own queue depth.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `alertmanager_notifications_failed_total` > 0 and on `alertmanager_notification_latency_seconds` p95 > 30s; synthetic canary alert fired every 5 min measuring click-to-pager wall time.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Operator Browser is in this design For a Prometheus-style monitoring system covering 10,000 servers, the whole point of collecting metrics is that a human — an SRE or on-call engineer — eventually needs to *see* them or be *woken up by* them. The Operator Browser is that human's window into the system: it renders Grafana dashboards when someone is investigating a problem, and it receives pager notifications when the alert engine decides something is on fire. Without modeling the browser as a real component, you'd miss the fact that monitoring has two very different read patterns sharing one TSDB — interactive dashboards (humans staring at charts) and automated alerts (machines deciding to page humans). ## What happens without thinking about it If the design ignores the browser, you get dashboards that technically work but feel broken: an operator clicks a dashboard during an incident, 20 panels fan out 20 parallel PromQL queries, the browser's 6-connection-per-origin limit queues them, and panels load in visible waves over 15 seconds. The operator, already stressed, can't tell if the system is slow or the monitoring is slow — and the TSDB takes the hit from redundant refreshes. ## The number that matters The capacity estimate says ~500 concurrent dashboards × 6 panels ≈ **3,000 PromQL queries/sec at peak**. That's the browser tier driving query load — roughly 5× the sustained sample *ingest* rate of 667K/s when you account for each query scanning many series. This is why Grafana needs query caching and why dashboards should cap panel count: the browsers, collectively, are the TSDB's biggest read client. ## The trade-off Putting humans in the loop via browsers means alert latency is bounded by human reaction time, not just pipeline latency — hence the <1 min pager SLO rather than something tighter.

app.name: Instrumented App
app.summary: Application process exposing a /metrics endpoint with counters, gauges, histograms, and summaries.

sections.heading: Exposition format
sections.body: Plain-text Prometheus exposition over HTTP: `http_requests_total{method="GET",status="200"} 1027`. OpenMetrics is the standardized superset.

sections.heading: Client library
sections.body: Language-native library (prometheus-client for Python, prom-client for Node, micrometer for JVM) maintains in-process counters atomically and serializes on scrape.

sections.heading: Cardinality discipline
sections.body: Never put user_id or request_id into a label — that explodes active series count. Use buckets (e.g., status_class="5xx" not full HTTP status).

sections.heading: Scrape cost
sections.body: Rendering /metrics is O(active series); a 1000-series endpoint serializes in <5ms. The app itself bears no cost in between scrapes.

gained: Fire-and-forget UDP — zero back-pressure on app
Works great for short-lived CLI jobs
lost: No service-discovery signal (can't tell 'target down' from 'target silent')
Aggregation happens outside the app — loss of per-process granularity
Heavier SDK than a simple Prometheus client
Collector infrastructure is another layer to run

bottlenecks.title: Label cardinality explosion from per-request IDs
bottlenecks.trigger: A developer adds a high-cardinality label like `user_id`, `request_id`, or raw `path` to a counter. With ~1000 active series/host baseline, a single service leaking user_id (say 100K distinct users) blows its per-process series count from ~1K to ~100K — and across 10K hosts this threatens the global 10M active-series budget.
bottlenecks.symptom: App memory grows unbounded (client library registry keeps every label combo forever); /metrics response balloons from ~18KB to multiple MB; scrape timeouts (>10s) cause `up=0` flapping; TSDB head block RAM spikes and triggers OOMs downstream.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce cardinality limits in the client library (e.g., prom-client `Registry` with a max-series guard), use bucketed labels (`status_class="5xx"` instead of raw status), move high-cardinality dimensions to exemplars or traces, and add CI linting (promtool check rules + custom metric-name/label linters) on PR.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `scrape_series_added` > 1000/scrape per target, `prometheus_tsdb_symbol_table_size_bytes` growth rate, and per-job `count({__name__=~".+"}) by (job)` crossing a per-service budget (e.g., 2000 series/instance).

bottlenecks.title: /metrics serialization stalls under GC / lock contention
bottlenecks.trigger: At 1000+ active series with histogram buckets, the client library serializes the registry under a read lock while the app holds 1000 concurrent in-flight requests updating counters. JVM/Go GC pauses or Python GIL contention during the 15s scrape tick can push /metrics response time past the collector's 10s timeout.
bottlenecks.symptom: Sporadic `up=0` for healthy instances; `scrape_duration_seconds` p99 jumps from <5ms to 8–12s during traffic bursts; gaps in dashboards despite the app serving real traffic fine.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use client libraries with lock-free/striped counters (Go prometheus/client_golang, Java micrometer with LongAdder), pre-allocate histogram buckets, keep bucket count ≤10 per histogram, and raise scrape_timeout to match p99 serialization (e.g., 15s) rather than default 10s.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `scrape_duration_seconds` p95/p99 per instance and alert on p99 > 2s; correlate with app-side GC pause metrics (`go_gc_duration_seconds`, JVM `jvm_gc_pause_seconds`).

bottlenecks.title: Counter loss on app restart / short-lived process
bottlenecks.trigger: In-process counters are memory-only. Any app restart, rolling deploy, or crash within the 15s scrape window loses the final delta. For a fleet with frequent deploys (say 100 pods/hr rolling across 10K hosts), thousands of counter increments are silently dropped per hour, and batch/CLI jobs exit before ever being scraped.
bottlenecks.symptom: `rate` and `increase` queries show visible dips or missed spikes aligned with deploy windows; reconciliation against logs/billing shows metrics undercount by 0.1–1%; short-lived jobs appear to have done nothing.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Route short-lived jobs through the Push Gateway (already in the design) with a unique `instance` label; for long-running apps, rely on Prometheus's built-in counter-reset detection in `rate` (automatic) and ensure graceful shutdown delays SIGTERM by > scrape_interval (15s+) so the final scrape lands.
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor `changes(process_start_time_seconds[1h])` per instance and alert on restarts clustered without a preceding successful scrape; track `pushgateway_http_requests_total` to confirm batch jobs are actually pushing.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Instrumented App is here For a monitoring system covering 10,000 servers, you have to answer a basic question: where do the numbers come from? In a pull-based Prometheus-style design, the answer is that *every application produces its own numbers* by exposing an HTTP endpoint at `/metrics`. The app itself is the source of truth — it's the only place that knows how many requests it handled, how long its DB calls took, or how many items are in its queue. There's no agent tailing logs, no sidecar guessing at internals; the app instruments itself with a client library (prom-client, micrometer, etc.) and the collector just scrapes it on a 15-second tick. ## What happens without it If apps aren't instrumented, the collector has nothing to pull. You'd be reduced to black-box probes (ping, TCP checks) and host-level stats (CPU, RAM) — which tell you a box is up, but not that its 5xx rate just spiked to 7% or that its p99 latency doubled. Operators would find out about incidents from customer complaints, not from the `HighErrorRate` alert rule, because that rule literally evaluates `http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}` — a counter that only exists because the app publishes it. ## The number that matters The capacity plan assumes **~1,000 active series per host × 10,000 hosts = 10M active series**. That 1,000 isn't arbitrary: it's what a typical service emits once you include per-endpoint counters and histogram buckets. Rendering 1,000 series serializes in <5ms, so the scrape cost on the app is negligible — which is exactly why pull-based works at this scale. ## The trade-off The designer accepted that every team must discipline their label cardinality (no `user_id` labels!) — because one careless service can blow the 10M-series budget for everyone.

pushgw.name: Push Gateway
pushgw.summary: Accumulator for short-lived batch jobs that finish before the next scrape.

sections.heading: When to use
sections.body: Cron jobs, CI builds, data-pipeline batches — anything that exits before the 15s scrape tick would otherwise lose its final metric.

sections.heading: API
sections.body:
```
PUT /metrics/job/{job_name}/instance/{instance}
# body: Prometheus exposition text
```
The collector then scrapes the push gateway like any other target.

sections.heading: Why not push for everything
sections.body: Pushed metrics outlive the process that produced them; stale values persist until explicitly deleted. This is a known footgun — Prometheus docs explicitly recommend the push gateway only for batch jobs.

bottlenecks.title: Stale metrics persist after job completion
bottlenecks.trigger: Batch jobs PUT metrics keyed by {job_name, instance} but never DELETE on exit (crash, OOM, kill -9, CI runner terminated mid-build). With thousands of services and frequent CI/cron runs, the push gateway accumulates series that the 15s collector scrape keeps re-ingesting into the 10M-active-series TSDB budget indefinitely.
bottlenecks.symptom: Alert rules fire on metrics from jobs that finished hours ago (e.g., `batch_last_success_timestamp` looks fresh but is frozen); dashboards show flat lines that aren't real; active series count drifts upward over weeks; operators discover 'ghost' instances that no longer exist in service discovery.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Require every batch job to DELETE its group on successful exit (`curl -X DELETE /metrics/job/{job}/instance/{instance}` in a trap handler), run a janitor that expires groups older than N hours, and include `push_time_seconds` in every push so alerts can gate on `time - push_time_seconds < 3600`. Never use the push gateway for long-running services.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `time - push_time_seconds{job=~".+"} > 2 * expected_run_interval` per job; track total group count on the pushgw (`pushgateway_build_info` + series count) and alert on unbounded growth; dashboard of groups with no DELETE in >24h.

bottlenecks.title: Single-instance SPOF and scrape bottleneck
bottlenecks.trigger: Push gateway is intentionally a singleton (it's a shared accumulator; HA would require external consensus on group state). The collector scrapes it on the same 15s tick as every other target, but a busy pushgw holding thousands of jobs' groups can serialize >100K series into a multi-MB /metrics response, pushing scrape latency past the 10s timeout.
bottlenecks.symptom: `up{job="pushgateway"} = 0` flapping; entire batch-job metrics pipeline goes dark during restarts or GC; scrape_duration_seconds for pushgw target climbs to 8–12s; CI pipelines fail to push during pushgw restart windows and silently lose their final metrics.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Shard push gateways by team/domain (one pushgw per ~500 jobs, fronted by a routing proxy on job_name hash) rather than one global instance; raise scrape_timeout for the pushgw target to 30s; run pushgw with persistence enabled (`--persistence.file`) so restarts don't lose in-flight groups; put it behind a load balancer with a persistent volume for fast failover.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `scrape_duration_seconds{job="pushgateway"}` p95 > 5s, `up{job="pushgateway"} == 0` for >30s, and `pushgateway_http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}` rate; track response body size via collector logs.

bottlenecks.title: Cardinality abuse from misused push gateway
bottlenecks.trigger: Teams discover push is easier than instrumenting a /metrics endpoint and start pushing per-request or per-CI-build metrics with unique labels (build_id, commit_sha, pr_number). With thousands of services across 10K hosts, even 100 builds/hr per service with unique build_id labels can add 100K+ series/day to the pushgw that then feed into the 10M active-series TSDB budget.
bottlenecks.symptom: Active series count on pushgw grows linearly with time rather than plateauing; TSDB head block RAM inflates; queries touching pushed metrics get slow because label index is huge; the 1.1 TB hot storage estimate is blown months early.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce a label allowlist at the pushgw (reverse proxy that rejects PUTs containing blocked label names like `build_id`, `commit_sha`, `trace_id`); document that pushgw is for aggregate job outcomes (`job_duration_seconds`, `job_success`), not per-run telemetry — those belong in logs/traces; add CI lint that rejects pushes with >10 distinct label values per key.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `count({job="pushgateway"}) by (job_name)` > 1000 per job; track `scrape_series_added{job="pushgateway"}` growth rate; weekly report of top-cardinality label keys on pushed series.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Push Gateway is here The core design choice in this monitoring system is **pull-based scraping**: every 15 seconds, the collector reaches out to each target's `/metrics` endpoint and grabs a snapshot. That works beautifully for long-running services — a web API handling requests 24/7 will always be there when the collector knocks. But across a fleet of 10,000 servers and thousands of services, there's a whole class of workloads that don't fit: cron jobs, CI builds, nightly ETL batches. These processes start, do their work, and exit — often in seconds. If a backup job runs in 8 seconds and the scrape interval is 15 seconds, the collector will never once catch it alive. Its metrics are invisible. ## What happens without it Without the push gateway, the metrics from short-lived jobs simply vanish. An operator writes an alert like "page me if the nightly backup fails" — but the `backup_last_success_timestamp` gauge never reaches the TSDB because the job was dead by the time the collector came knocking. The alert engine has nothing to evaluate against, and the SRE team finds out about the failed backup from a customer, not the pager. ## The scale argument The design targets a **15-second scrape interval**. Any job with a lifetime shorter than ~30 seconds (one scrape plus margin) has a meaningful probability of being missed entirely. Across thousands of services running hourly/nightly batch jobs, that's potentially thousands of blind spots per day. The push gateway accepts a `PUT /metrics/job/{name}` from the job *before it exits*, holds the value, and lets the collector scrape *it* on the normal 15s tick. ## The trade-off The designer accepted that pushed metrics outlive their producer — a known footgun where stale values linger until explicitly deleted — because the alternative (blindness to batch workloads) is worse.

collector.name: Scrape Collector
collector.summary: Prometheus-style scraper: on every interval, pulls /metrics from every discovered target.

sections.heading: Service discovery
sections.body: Targets come from Kubernetes API, Consul, EC2 tags, or a static file. The collector recomputes its target set every 30s. A target dropping out flips `up{instance=...} = 0` — a first-class signal.

sections.heading: Scrape loop
sections.body: For each target: `GET /metrics` with a 10s timeout, parse exposition format, attach `{job,instance}` labels, forward to Kafka (or write directly to TSDB in a simpler deploy).

sections.heading: Sharding
sections.body: One collector instance per ~2000 targets. Horizontal sharding via hash(instance) keeps per-collector scrape load even.

sections.heading: Staleness markers
sections.body: When a target disappears from service discovery, the collector writes a synthetic stale sample so alert evaluators know the series ended (not just paused).

gained: No local TSDB — just forwards to remote TSDB
lost: No local query / alerting — central outage = blind

bottlenecks.title: Scrape fan-out saturates collector's HTTP client pool
bottlenecks.trigger: Each collector shard owns ~2000 targets and must complete all scrapes within the 15s interval. With a 10s scrape timeout and 100-way parallelism per worker, a tail of slow targets (GC pauses, /metrics serialization at 1000+ series) keeps connections held and starves the scheduler — 2000 targets / 100 parallel × avg 200ms = 4s ideal, but p99 spikes to 8–12s push total wall time past 15s.
bottlenecks.symptom: Scrape interval skew increases (actual interval 18–25s instead of 15s); `up{}=0` flaps on healthy targets due to 10s timeouts; gaps appear in rate queries; collector CPU pinned at 100% on a few cores while most sit idle.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Raise per-collector parallelism to 500–1000 concurrent scrapes (tune `GOMAXPROCS` and HTTP transport `MaxIdleConnsPerHost`); reshard hotter jobs to more collector instances (target ≤1500 targets/shard when series/target is high); set `scrape_timeout` just below `scrape_interval` (e.g., 12s); enable HTTP keep-alive across scrape ticks.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `prometheus_target_interval_length_seconds{quantile="0.99"}` > 1.2× configured interval; track `scrape_duration_seconds` p99 per job and `up` flap rate; monitor Go `http.Transport` idle conn metrics.

bottlenecks.title: Service discovery churn causes target-set recompute storms
bottlenecks.trigger: The collector recomputes its target set every 30s from Kubernetes/Consul. In a fleet of 10K hosts with frequent pod rollouts (100+ pods/hr), a large rollout can churn hundreds of targets per SD refresh. Each change triggers relabeling rule evaluation across all targets and writes staleness markers downstream.
bottlenecks.symptom: CPU spikes every 30s correlated with SD refresh; scrapes briefly stall during target-set swap; bursts of `up=0` staleness markers flood Kafka; newly-created pods aren't scraped until the next SD tick, creating up to 30s blind windows during deploys.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use watch-based SD (Kubernetes informer, Consul blocking queries) instead of 30s polling so changes stream incrementally; cache relabel rule output keyed by target hash to avoid recomputing for unchanged targets; shard SD clients so no single collector watches the full fleet.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `prometheus_sd_kubernetes_events_total` rate spikes, `prometheus_target_sync_length_seconds` p95 > 1s, and gaps between target-creation-timestamp and first successful scrape > 15s.

bottlenecks.title: Kafka producer back-pressure stalls the scrape loop
bottlenecks.trigger: Collector produces ~1M samples/sec peak across 200 Kafka partitions keyed by hash(series_id). If the Kafka cluster is compacting, a broker fails over, or one partition gets a hot series (cardinality spike on a single job), the producer's in-memory buffer (default ~32MB) fills and `produce` starts blocking. Scrape workers block on Kafka instead of moving to the next target.
bottlenecks.symptom: Scrape duration inflates uniformly across all targets (not just slow apps); collector memory grows until OOM; `up=0` across entire jobs despite targets being healthy; end-to-end ingest lag on dashboards climbs from seconds to minutes.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Configure producer with `linger.ms=50`, `batch.size=1MB`, `buffer.memory=256MB`, and `max.block.ms=1000` so producer fails fast instead of blocking scrapes; decouple scrape from produce with a bounded in-memory ring buffer (drop-oldest on overflow with a counter metric); partition by `hash(job, instance)` rather than per-series to keep partition count aligned with shard fan-in.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `kafka_producer_buffer_available_bytes` < 20% for >1 min, `kafka_producer_record_send_rate` drop correlated with `scrape_duration_seconds` increase, and any non-zero `collector_samples_dropped_total`.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Scrape Collector is here For a monitoring system covering 10,000 servers and thousands of services, *something* has to actually go fetch the numbers from every app's `/metrics` endpoint on a regular schedule. That's the collector's entire job. The design commits to **pull-based** monitoring — instead of apps pushing data whenever they feel like it, the collector reaches out to each target every 15 seconds. This choice is load-bearing: because the collector learns its target list from service discovery (Kubernetes, Consul), a target that *should* exist but doesn't respond flips `up{instance=...} = 0`, which is itself a first-class alerting signal. You get "is the app dead?" for free from the same mechanism that collects metrics. ## What happens without it If there's no collector, apps have nowhere to send their `/metrics` exposition — the `Instrumented App` component exposes an HTTP endpoint but no one calls it, so samples never make it to Kafka or the TSDB. Dashboards in Grafana would be empty, and alert rules would evaluate against nothing and silently never fire. The operator's first clue would be a customer complaint, not a pager. ## The number that matters The design ingests **~667K samples/sec sustained** (10M active series ÷ 15s scrape interval). One collector shard handles ~2000 targets; at ~1000 series per target, that's 2M samples every 15s per shard, or ~133K samples/sec — so you need roughly **5 collector shards** to cover the fleet, with headroom for the 1M/sec peak. ## Trade-off Pull-based scraping means the collector must discover and reach every target on the network — harder across firewalls and NATs than letting apps push outward.

kafka.name: Metrics Kafka
kafka.summary: Optional buffer between collectors and the TSDB write path — absorbs bursts and decouples failure domains.

sections.heading: Why a queue in the middle
sections.body: TSDB writes are the most expensive step; a Kafka buffer lets collectors keep scraping even if the TSDB is compacting or failing over. Retention: 4h — long enough to ride out a TSDB outage.

sections.heading: Partitioning
sections.body: Partition by `hash(series_id)` so all samples for a series land on the same TSDB shard consumer. 200 partitions support >1M samples/sec comfortably.

sections.heading: Skip-the-queue mode
sections.body: In small Prometheus deployments, collectors remote-write directly to the TSDB. Kafka becomes valuable at the 100K+ samples/sec scale where TSDB writes start fluctuating.

lost: A TSDB stall back-pressures collectors; scrapes start to miss
No replay window if TSDB corruption needs a backfill

bottlenecks.title: Hot partition from hash(series_id) skew
bottlenecks.trigger: With 200 partitions and ~1M samples/sec peak, the ideal per-partition rate is ~5K samples/sec. But hash(series_id) partitioning means a handful of very high-frequency series (e.g., a `node_cpu_seconds_total` on every one of 10K hosts, or a cardinality-spiking job emitting 50K new series) can concentrate 10–50x the average load on 1–2 partitions.
bottlenecks.symptom: Per-partition producer latency p99 jumps from <10ms to 100ms+; consumer lag on hot partitions grows to minutes while cold partitions sit at zero; TSDB consumer for the hot partition falls behind, delaying dashboard freshness for popular metrics; ISR shrinks on the hot partition's leader broker.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Repartition on `hash(job, instance)` instead of `hash(series_id)` to spread a single target's ~1000 series across partitions while keeping per-series ordering within one target; raise partition count to 400–600 so rebalancing has finer granularity; monitor and manually reassign hot partitions to less-loaded brokers via `kafka-reassign-partitions`.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `kafka.log.Log.Size` or `MessagesInPerSec` stddev across partitions > 3x mean; track consumer lag per partition and alert when any partition lag > 10x median; dashboard of top-10 partitions by bytes-in/sec.

bottlenecks.title: Broker disk exhaustion from 4h retention at peak ingest
bottlenecks.trigger: At 1M samples/sec peak with ~100 bytes/record on the wire (uncompressed exposition-derived JSON with labels), raw ingest is ~100 MB/sec × 4h retention × 3x replication = ~4.3 TB of log storage cluster-wide. A TSDB outage that causes backlog accumulation, or a cardinality incident doubling sample size, can blow past provisioned disk in hours.
bottlenecks.symptom: Brokers hit disk-full, start rejecting produces with `NotEnoughReplicasException`; collectors back-pressure and miss scrape ticks; emergency log-segment deletion causes silent sample loss; cluster-wide produce latency spikes as remaining brokers take extra load.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable producer-side compression (`compression.type=zstd`) which typically yields 5–10x reduction on label-heavy metric records; set `log.retention.bytes` per partition as a hard cap in addition to time-based retention; provision 2x headroom over peak × retention; add tiered storage (Kafka 3.6+ KIP-405) so older segments offload to S3.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `kafka.log.Log.Size` per broker > 70% of disk; track `BytesInPerSec` vs configured `log.retention.bytes` ratio; alert on any broker with <24h of runway at current ingest rate.

bottlenecks.title: Controller/ISR churn during broker failover at 200-partition scale
bottlenecks.trigger: With 200 partitions × 3 replicas = 600 partition replicas, a single broker failure in a typical 5-broker cluster triggers leader election for ~40 partitions simultaneously. At 1M samples/sec, each second of unavailability loses ~5000 samples per partition unless producers buffer.
bottlenecks.symptom: Collectors see `LEADER_NOT_AVAILABLE` errors for 5–30s during rolling restarts or broker crashes; producer buffers fill and start blocking scrape workers (see collector bottlenecks); brief sample gap visible on dashboards as a flat line across many series simultaneously.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Run KRaft mode (Kafka 3.3+) instead of ZooKeeper for faster controller failover (<1s vs 5–10s); set producer `acks=all` with `retries=Integer.MAX_VALUE` and `delivery.timeout.ms=120000` so transient leader changes are absorbed by client retry; use `min.insync.replicas=2` with RF=3 so one broker loss never blocks writes; pre-warm page cache on new leaders.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `kafka.controller.ActiveControllerCount!= 1` cluster-wide, `UnderReplicatedPartitions > 0` for >2min, and `LeaderElectionRateAndTimeMs` spikes; track producer-side `record-error-rate` and `record-retry-rate` per collector.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why Kafka sits between the collectors and the TSDB In this Prometheus-style monitoring system, the collectors scrape 10,000 hosts every 15 seconds — they *cannot* pause. If the TSDB is compacting a block, failing over a leader, or just slow for 90 seconds, the collectors still have to deliver the next scrape cycle on time. Without a buffer in between, a hiccup at the TSDB back-pressures the collector, which then misses scrape ticks, which flips `up=0` on healthy targets and fires false alerts. Kafka absorbs that mismatch: collectors produce at a steady rate, the TSDB consumes at whatever rate it can, and the 4-hour retention window gives you room to replay if something downstream corrupts or needs a backfill. ## What breaks without it Imagine the TSDB head block hits an OOM and restarts — a 60-second outage. Without Kafka, every collector's remote-write buffer fills, scrapes queue up, and within a minute you have fleet-wide gaps in dashboards *and* a storm of bogus "target down" pages. The operator can't tell real incidents from monitoring-system incidents. With Kafka, the TSDB just resumes consuming from its last committed offset and catches up; the collectors never noticed. ## The number that justifies it The design ingests **~667K samples/sec sustained, ~1M/sec peak**. Partitioning across 200 Kafka partitions gives ~5K samples/sec/partition — trivial for Kafka, but critical decoupling because a single TSDB shard stalling for 60s means 60M buffered samples that Kafka can hold comfortably (200 partitions × 4h retention handles billions). The trade-off: one more distributed system to operate, accepted because at this scale a direct write path makes the TSDB a single point of back-pressure.

tsdb.name: Time Series DB
tsdb.summary: Columnar TSDB (Prometheus local + Thanos/Mimir for long-term) with Gorilla compression.

sections.heading: Data model
sections.body: Each series keyed by `{metric_name, label_set}`, storing `(timestamp, float64)` pairs. Active-series count, not sample count, dominates memory.

sections.heading: Compression
sections.body: Delta-of-delta timestamp encoding + XOR float encoding (Facebook Gorilla, 2015) → ~1.3 B/sample from ~16 B raw. 10x storage reduction.

sections.heading: Write path
sections.body: Samples first go to an in-memory head block (2h), WAL for durability. Head block is periodically compacted to immutable 2h blocks on disk, then merged into larger blocks.

sections.heading: Query path (PromQL)
sections.body: PromQL resolves the series matching the label selectors, then streams samples through the rate/avg/sum pipeline. Typical dashboard query: `rate(http_requests_total{job="api"}[5m])` over 1h = 12 points/series * matching series.

sections.heading: Long-term storage
sections.body: After 15 days local, blocks ship to S3 (Thanos/Mimir). Queries spanning old + new fan out to both stores and merge.

lost: License shifts in OSS vs Enterprise have been contentious
Cardinality handling historically weaker than Prometheus

gained: Horizontally scalable with simpler ops than Thanos
Unified OLAP for logs + metrics + traces
Extreme compression on large historical ranges
lost: No native PromQL — need a translator (chproxy / PromQL → SQL)

bottlenecks.title: Head block RAM blows up from active-series growth
bottlenecks.trigger: Design budgets 10M active series, but each series holds an in-memory head chunk plus label-index entries (~3–10 KB/series). At 10M series that's 30–100 GB of head+index RAM; a cardinality incident (e.g., an app leaking user_id labels, see the app component) can double active series within one 2h head window before compaction sheds it.
bottlenecks.symptom: TSDB OOM-kills mid-day; on restart it replays a multi-GB WAL for 10–30 minutes during which queries return partial data; `up` gaps across the fleet; Grafana dashboards show ragged flat lines; alert engine evaluates against incomplete data and either misses fires or emits false `up=0` pages.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce per-tenant/job series limits via Mimir/Cortex `max_global_series_per_user` or Prometheus `--storage.tsdb.head-chunks-write-queue-size` + ingestion relabel drops; shard the TSDB horizontally (hashmod on series_id) so each shard holds ≤2M series; shorten head block to 1h in extreme cases; pre-provision 2x RAM headroom over projected steady-state; add admission-time cardinality rejection at the write path.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `prometheus_tsdb_head_series` > 80% of budget per shard, `prometheus_tsdb_head_series_created_total` rate spikes >10K/min, `process_resident_memory_bytes` > 70% of node RAM, and `scrape_series_added` p99 per target.

bottlenecks.title: High-cardinality PromQL queries starve the query engine
bottlenecks.trigger: Grafana issues ~3K PromQL/sec peak (500 dashboards × 6 panels). A single badly-written query like `sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m]))` without a `by` clause or job filter touches all matching series across the 10M-series index; a 1h range at 15s step over 100K matching series = 24M sample reads + label-index scan. A handful of these concurrently exhaust the query concurrency pool (default Prometheus `--query.max-concurrency=20`).
bottlenecks.symptom: Dashboard panels hang or 504; `query_range` p99 climbs from ~20ms to 5–30s; queued queries pile up behind a few heavy ones; alert rule evaluations (which share the same query engine) miss their 30s tick and delay pages past the 1 min SLO; operator sees 'query processing would load too many samples' errors.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce `--query.max-samples=50000000` and short `--query.timeout=30s`; deploy a query frontend (Thanos Query Frontend / Mimir query-frontend) with splitting-by-interval + result caching; separate the alert evaluator's query path from Grafana's (dedicated ruler pool) so dashboard abuse can't delay pages; block anonymous label-wide queries via a PromQL linter; educate teams to always include `by (job)` or a job filter.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `prometheus_engine_query_duration_seconds` p99 > 2s, `prometheus_engine_queries_concurrent_max - prometheus_engine_queries` < 3 for >1 min, any query returning >1M samples in `prometheus_engine_query_samples_total`, and rule group evaluation duration > 30s interval.

bottlenecks.title: Compaction + remote-write to long-term store stalls the write path
bottlenecks.trigger: Every 2h the head block compacts to disk and, after 15d, blocks ship to Thanos/Mimir on S3. At 57.6B samples/day × 1.3B = ~75 GB/day of block writes per replica plus background merges of older blocks. A slow S3 upload, disk saturation during merge of a 24h block, or a Thanos sidecar backlog causes WAL truncation to lag, which then pressures the head and bounces back into ingest.
bottlenecks.symptom: Disk I/O wait climbs to 40%+ during compaction windows; `prometheus_tsdb_wal_truncations_failed_total` increments; WAL grows from ~1 GB steady-state to 10+ GB; Kafka consumer lag on the TSDB consumer climbs to minutes; after block ship failures, local retention silently extends past 15d and fills disk.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use NVMe for the TSDB data dir (head + WAL + blocks), separate WAL device from block device if on SATA; tune `--storage.tsdb.max-block-chunk-segment-size` and stagger compaction across replicas so they don't compact in sync; run Thanos sidecar with bounded upload concurrency and alert on its lag; provision block storage for 2x the 15d × 75 GB/day = 1.1 TB budget to absorb ship backlogs; use vertical compaction only off-hours.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `prometheus_tsdb_compactions_failed_total` > 0, `prometheus_tsdb_compaction_duration_seconds` p99 > 30min, `thanos_shipper_uploads_total` rate drop to 0 for >30min, disk utilization > 75%, and `prometheus_tsdb_wal_corruptions_total` > 0.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a purpose-built TSDB for this problem For a monitoring system watching 10,000 servers, you're dealing with a very specific data shape: huge numbers of series, each getting a new `(timestamp, float)` pair every 15 seconds, forever. A general-purpose database like Postgres or MongoDB would technically store this, but it would be catastrophically wasteful — a row-per-sample design means per-row overhead (indexes, tuple headers, transaction metadata) dwarfs the actual 16 bytes of data. At this scale, storage and memory efficiency aren't nice-to-haves; they're the entire game. The TSDB exists because time-series data has exploitable structure — timestamps arrive monotonically, adjacent floats are usually close in value — and Gorilla compression (delta-of-delta + XOR) squeezes samples down to **~1.3 bytes each**, roughly 10× better than naive storage. ## What goes wrong without it Drop the TSDB in favor of a generic OLTP database and two things break at once. First, ingest: at 667K samples/sec sustained, a Postgres-style writer would spend all its time on WAL and index maintenance and fall behind within minutes, back-pressuring Kafka until collectors start dropping scrapes. Second, queries: Grafana panels like `rate(http_requests_total[5m])` need to stream thousands of samples per series through a pipeline — a TSDB does this in tens of milliseconds because samples for one series are stored contiguously; a generic DB would do random I/O per point and panels would take 30+ seconds. ## The number that forces the choice Daily volume is **57.6 billion samples/day**. At 1.3 B/sample with 15-day retention: 57.6B × 1.3 × 15 ≈ **1.1 TB**. At 16 B/sample (uncompressed) that's **13.8 TB** — an order of magnitude more hardware, for the exact same observability. The trade-off: you give up SQL and general-purpose querying for PromQL, which only understands time-series shapes — fine, because that's all you're storing.

alertengine.name: Alert Rule Engine
alertengine.summary: Continuously evaluates alert rules (PromQL) and hands firing alerts to the notifier.

sections.heading: Evaluation loop
sections.body: Every 30s: for each alert rule, run the PromQL expression against the TSDB. If the result is non-empty for `for:` duration, transition the alert from `pending` to `firing`.

sections.heading: Rule example
sections.body:
```
alert: HighErrorRate
expr: | sum(rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m])) by (job) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m])) by (job) > 0.05
for: 10m
labels: { severity: "page" }
annotations: { summary: "5xx rate > 5% on {{ $labels.job }}" }
```

sections.heading: Grouping and inhibition
sections.body: Alertmanager groups alerts by label (e.g., all DB-down alerts into one page) and inhibits downstream alerts when an upstream is firing (inhibit `HighLatency` if `DBDown` is firing).

sections.heading: Dedup / repeat interval
sections.body: After firing once, repeat every 4h until resolved. Silencing and maintenance windows suppress delivery without losing state.

gained: Unified with dashboards; multi-data-source rules (not only Prometheus)
lost: Younger than Alertmanager; fewer operator patterns documented

bottlenecks.title: Rule group evaluation overruns the 30s interval
bottlenecks.trigger: With 2000 rules / 30s = ~67 evals/sec and rules sharing a single query engine pool, a handful of heavy rules (e.g., unfiltered `sum(rate(...))` over 10M active series) or a TSDB query slowdown pushes per-group evaluation past the 30s tick. Rule groups are sequential within a group, so one slow rule delays every subsequent rule in that group.
bottlenecks.symptom: `prometheus_rule_group_last_duration_seconds` exceeds `prometheus_rule_group_interval_seconds`; alerts fire 60–120s late, blowing the <1 min pager SLO; `for:` duration effectively lengthens because the state machine only advances on successful evals; some alerts appear to 'skip' evaluations during TSDB pressure.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Split the 2000 rules across many small rule groups (≤50 rules/group) so slow rules only block their own group; shard the ruler horizontally (Mimir/Cortex ruler) by tenant or rule-group hash; precompute expensive expressions via recording rules (`job:http_errors:rate5m`) so alert rules evaluate cheap instant queries; give the ruler a dedicated TSDB query frontend pool separate from Grafana's 3K/sec dashboard load.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `prometheus_rule_group_last_duration_seconds / prometheus_rule_group_interval_seconds > 0.8`, `prometheus_rule_evaluation_failures_total > 0`, and `prometheus_rule_group_iterations_missed_total` increasing; dashboard p99 rule eval duration per group.

bottlenecks.title: Alert storm from correlated failure flattens the notifier pipeline
bottlenecks.trigger: A single infra incident (bad deploy, AZ outage, DNS flap) trips many rules at once — e.g., `up=0` across 2000 instances plus downstream `HighErrorRate` on every dependent job. With ~50 firing on average but thousands possible during correlated incidents, the engine emits 10K+ alerts in one 30s tick, overwhelming Alertmanager's gossip dedup and the notifier's 200-concurrency webhook pool.
bottlenecks.symptom: On-call gets paged 500+ times for one root cause; Slack channels become unusable; PagerDuty rate-limits the integration key (429s); Alertmanager gossip CPU pegs at 100% reconciling cluster state; critical alerts queue behind noise and arrive 10+ minutes late; some alerts silently dropped when notifier retries exhaust.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Aggressive grouping in Alertmanager (`group_by: [alertname, cluster]`, `group_wait: 30s`, `group_interval: 5m`) to collapse correlated alerts into single notifications; inhibition rules so `up=0` suppresses downstream `HighErrorRate` / `HighLatency` on the same instance; hierarchical alerts (cluster-level `ClusterDown` inhibits instance-level `InstanceDown`); cap notifier concurrency per receiver and use circuit breakers on provider webhooks.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `ALERTS{alertstate="firing"}` count > 100 (meta-alert), `alertmanager_notifications_failed_total` rate > 0, `alertmanager_dispatcher_aggregation_groups` spike, and PagerDuty 429 responses in notifier logs.

bottlenecks.title: State loss on engine restart causes `for:` clause resets
bottlenecks.trigger: Alert state (pending since, active_since) is held in memory. A restart during deploy, OOM, or leader failover resets every pending alert's `active_since` clock. With 2000 rules and many using `for: 10m` or longer, a restart during an active incident effectively extends alert latency by another 10m as rules re-enter pending.
bottlenecks.symptom: Operator deploys ruler config change at minute 7 of a 10m `for:` window — pager never fires because active_since resets; post-incident timeline shows condition was true for 18 minutes before the page; duplicate or missed resolves when HA replicas disagree on state after a partition.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Run HA ruler pairs with gossip-based state sharing (Alertmanager + Prometheus HA pair, or Mimir ruler with persistent state in object storage); drain-and-handoff on rolling restart (SIGTERM wait > longest `for:` window); persist pending-alert state to disk (Prometheus `--rules.alert.resend-delay` + external state store); prefer recording-rule-based alerts which recover faster from restart since the underlying series is already computed.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `process_start_time_seconds` changes for the ruler (restart tracker) correlated with any rule group entering pending; track divergence between HA ruler replicas via `ALERTS` series compared by `prometheus_replica`; synthetic canary alert that measures end-to-end `for:` adherence across restarts.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Alert Rule Engine is here For a monitoring system watching 10,000 servers, collecting metrics is only half the job — someone (or something) has to *notice* when those metrics indicate trouble. No human is going to stare at Grafana dashboards 24/7 waiting for the 5xx rate on the payments service to creep past 5%. The Alert Rule Engine is the piece that continuously asks the TSDB questions like "is the error rate above threshold right now?" on a fixed schedule, and escalates to a human only when the answer has been "yes" for long enough to rule out a blip. Without it, the TSDB is just a very expensive historical archive. ## What happens without it The TSDB would still faithfully record that the payments service started emitting 7% 5xx errors at 2:14 AM — but nobody would know until an on-call engineer happened to open a dashboard, or, more likely, a customer filed a support ticket. Grafana shows the incident beautifully in hindsight. The collector keeps scraping. The notifier has nothing to send. Mean time to detection goes from ~10 minutes to however long it takes a customer to complain. ## The number that matters The design has **2,000 alert rules evaluated every 30 seconds** — that's ~67 rule evaluations/sec, each a small PromQL query against the TSDB. Compare that to Grafana's 3,000 PromQL/sec peak: alerting is a modest but *relentless* query load that must never pause, which is why it gets its own dedicated engine rather than being bolted onto dashboards. ## Trade-off The designer accepted a minimum ~30-second detection floor (eval interval) plus the rule's `for:` duration, trading instant reaction for fewer false pages from transient spikes.

grafana.name: Grafana
grafana.summary: Visualization layer. Issues PromQL queries to the TSDB and renders time-series panels.

sections.heading: Query fan-out
sections.body: A dashboard with 6 panels over a 1h range at 30s step issues 6 PromQL queries; each returns at most 120 points/series. Grafana pipelines them in parallel.

sections.heading: Caching
sections.body: Dashboard JSON is cached in the browser; query results are NOT cached by default — every refresh hits the TSDB. Enterprise Grafana has a query cache for ranges older than now.

sections.heading: Variables
sections.body: Template variables (e.g., `$job`, `$instance`) do a `label_values(...)` query on dashboard load. High-cardinality label dropdowns are a common source of slow dashboards.

lost: Smaller community; fewer prebuilt dashboards than Grafana

bottlenecks.title: Uncached query fan-out overwhelms TSDB at peak dashboard load
bottlenecks.trigger: Grafana does not cache query results by default; with 500 concurrent dashboards × 6 panels = 3,000 PromQL/sec peak, every user refresh or auto-refresh tick (default 30s) re-issues all range queries. A single dashboard set to 5s refresh with 20 panels alone contributes 240 PromQL/sec.
bottlenecks.symptom: TSDB query engine saturates (`--query.max-concurrency=20` queue fills), panel p99 climbs from ~200ms to 10–30s, Grafana shows 'query timeout' or partial panels, and alert rule evaluations sharing the same TSDB miss their 30s tick causing pager SLO breaches.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Deploy Thanos/Mimir query-frontend in front of the TSDB with split-by-interval and result caching (Memcached/Redis), enable Grafana Enterprise query caching for ranges older than now-step, cap dashboard auto-refresh to ≥30s, and enforce `$__rate_interval` / `$__interval` so step scales with range instead of hardcoded 15s.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `grafana_datasource_request_duration_seconds` p99 per datasource, alert when >2s for 5 min; monitor TSDB `prometheus_engine_queries_concurrent_max - prometheus_engine_queries` < 3; dashboard cache hit ratio (expect >70% steady-state once enabled).

bottlenecks.title: High-cardinality template variable queries stall dashboard load
bottlenecks.trigger: Template variables issue `label_values(instance)` or `label_values(pod)` on dashboard open against a TSDB holding 10M active series across 10K hosts. A single unscoped `label_values(instance)` scans the full label index and returns 10K+ entries; chained variables (job → instance → endpoint) multiply the cost.
bottlenecks.symptom: Dashboard is blank for 3–10s after navigation while variable dropdowns resolve; occasional 504 from Grafana datasource proxy (default 30s timeout); incident-time dashboards slowest exactly when operators need them; `$instance` dropdown truncated or unusable.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Always scope variable queries with a job filter (`label_values(up{job="$job"}, instance)`), set variable refresh to 'On Dashboard Load' not 'On Time Range Change', raise Grafana's datasource `timeout` only as last resort, and forbid variables on labels with >1K distinct values via dashboard linting (grafonnet/dashboard-linter in CI).
bottlenecks.detection: Log `/api/v1/label/*/values` requests with latency > 1s or response size > 5,000 entries; alert on Grafana `grafana_http_request_duration_seconds{handler=~"/api/datasources/proxy/.+"}` p95 > 3s; track per-dashboard load time from browser RUM.

bottlenecks.title: Datasource proxy connection pool exhaustion under panel fan-out
bottlenecks.trigger: Grafana proxies every panel query through its backend to the TSDB (single datasource URL). At 3K PromQL/sec peak with default Go `http.Transport` settings (`MaxIdleConnsPerHost=2`, `MaxConnsPerHost=0`), bursts of 100+ simultaneous panel queries from a single dashboard refresh saturate the TCP connection pool to the TSDB endpoint.
bottlenecks.symptom: Queries queue inside the Grafana process before even hitting the TSDB; panels load in visible waves of ~10 despite the TSDB being idle; `grafana_datasource_request_duration_seconds` includes 100–500ms of pure wait time; CPU low on both Grafana and TSDB but latency high.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Tune the datasource to use HTTP/2 (multiplexed streams over one connection), raise `MaxIdleConnsPerHost` to 100+ via Grafana's `dataproxy.max_conns_per_host` config, run multiple Grafana replicas behind a load balancer (shard by org/team), and prefer direct browser→TSDB with CORS rather than proxying when auth model allows.
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor Grafana `http_client_requests_active` / `go_goroutines` spikes during dashboard load; compare `grafana_datasource_request_duration_seconds` to TSDB-reported `prometheus_engine_query_duration_seconds` — any gap >50ms indicates proxy-side queuing.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why Grafana is here For a monitoring system watching 10,000 servers, the TSDB holds billions of samples a day — but humans can't read PromQL results as JSON during an incident at 2 AM. Grafana is the piece that turns `sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m])) by (job)` into a line chart an SRE can glance at and recognize the shape of. It's also the shared language across teams: dashboards become the artifacts that teams link to in runbooks, postmortems, and Slack threads. Without it, the TSDB is technically complete but operationally useless — you'd be `curl`ing `/api/v1/query_range` and piping it to `jq`. ## What breaks without it The alert engine would still page on-call, but the on-call engineer has nowhere to go to *investigate*. They get a pager for `HighErrorRate` on the payments service and then... squint at raw PromQL in a terminal? Mean time to resolution balloons from minutes to hours because nobody can see the correlated metrics — CPU, latency, upstream error rates — side by side. The TSDB takes the hit indirectly: operators write worse, heavier ad-hoc queries trying to reconstruct what a dashboard would have shown in one glance. ## The number that matters The design estimates **500 concurrent dashboards × 6 panels ≈ 3,000 PromQL/sec peak** from Grafana. That's ~4.5× the sustained ingest rate of 667K samples/sec — meaning the *read* path through Grafana is the TSDB's heaviest client, justifying dedicated query-frontend caching in front of it. ## Trade-off The designer accepted that uncached dashboard refreshes can overwhelm the TSDB, in exchange for visualizations being a first-class part of the incident-response workflow.

notifier.name: Notification Sender
notifier.summary: Routes firing alerts to PagerDuty, Slack, email, and webhooks.

sections.heading: Routes
sections.body: Label-based tree: `severity=page` → PagerDuty; `severity=ticket` → Jira; `team=data` → #data-alerts Slack. Same alert can fan out to multiple channels.

sections.heading: Delivery
sections.body: HTTP POST to provider webhook with an integration key. Retries with exponential backoff up to 6h — alerts must survive transient provider outages.

sections.heading: On-call rotation
sections.body: PagerDuty owns the schedule. Alertmanager just hands off — the escalation policy is external.

bottlenecks.title: Provider webhook rate limits during alert storms
bottlenecks.trigger: With ~50 firing on average but correlated incidents (AZ outage, bad deploy) pushing `up=0` across 2000+ instances plus downstream rules, the notifier can be asked to deliver 10K+ webhooks in a 30s eval tick. PagerDuty's Events API v2 rate-limits at ~120 events/min per integration key, and Slack webhooks at ~1 msg/sec per hook — both are blown through in seconds.
bottlenecks.symptom: On-call gets a flood of pages for a single root cause, then later critical alerts are delayed 5–30 min as the notifier retries 429s with exponential backoff; Slack messages arrive out of order or never; PagerDuty incidents stack up with duplicate dedup_keys; the <1 min pager SLO is violated across the board.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Aggressive Alertmanager grouping (`group_by: [alertname, cluster]`, `group_wait: 30s`, `group_interval: 5m`, `repeat_interval: 4h`) to collapse correlated alerts into one notification; inhibition rules so `ClusterDown` suppresses instance-level `InstanceDown`; per-receiver concurrency caps and circuit breakers on provider webhooks; multiple PagerDuty integration keys sharded by team to multiply the rate-limit budget.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `alertmanager_notifications_failed_total{integration=~"pagerduty|slack"}` rate > 0, HTTP 429 response count in notifier logs, `alertmanager_notification_latency_seconds` p95 > 30s, and a meta-alert on `count(ALERTS{alertstate="firing"}) > 100`.

bottlenecks.title: Webhook concurrency pool saturation under sustained notification load
bottlenecks.trigger: Notifier sim shows concurrency=200 with per-webhook serviceTimeMs=50–300 (p99 likely >500ms to external providers over TLS). Sustained throughput ceiling is ~200 / 0.2s = 1000 webhooks/sec, but a single provider slowdown (PagerDuty p99 climbing to 2s) drops effective throughput to ~100/sec — below the burst rate from even modest correlated firings.
bottlenecks.symptom: Notification queue depth grows; alerts that fired at t=0 get delivered at t+2min or later; later-arriving critical alerts queue behind lower-severity Jira/email tickets already in flight; on-call sees pager arrive well after the Slack message from the same alert.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Separate worker pools per receiver type (dedicated high-priority pool for `severity=page` with 100 workers, separate pool for ticket/email) so a slow Jira receiver can't starve PagerDuty; use per-receiver bounded queues with priority ordering on alert severity label; set aggressive HTTP client timeouts (5s connect, 10s total) with fast retry rather than long blocking waits; scale notifier replicas horizontally behind Alertmanager's gossip cluster.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `alertmanager_notification_queue_length` per receiver, `alertmanager_notification_latency_seconds` p95/p99 broken down by integration, HTTP client in-flight request gauge, and alert when any receiver's queue depth > 500 or latency p95 > 10s for 2 min.

bottlenecks.title: Retry-induced duplicate pages during provider flap
bottlenecks.trigger: Design specifies retries with exponential backoff up to 6h. If PagerDuty returns 5xx or times out mid-delivery (after accepting the request but before acking), the notifier retries — but the incident was already created. Over a 6h retry window during a provider flap, a single alert can generate 10+ duplicate pages across retries if `dedup_key` isn't set consistently.
bottlenecks.symptom: On-call phone rings repeatedly for the same underlying incident; PagerDuty shows multiple open incidents for one alert; operators waste cycles acknowledging/merging duplicates during an active incident; trust in the pager degrades ("just ignore the 3rd ring, it's the same thing").
bottlenecks.mitigation: Always set PagerDuty `dedup_key` to a stable hash of `{alertname, grouping_labels}` (as shown in the existing flow with `dedup_key: "HighErrorRate/payments"`); use idempotency keys on all webhook POSTs; cap retry window to 1h (not 6h) for page-severity since stale pages are worse than missed ones; run HA Alertmanager pair with gossip so one replica's retry state is visible to the other, preventing both from re-sending after partition heal.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on PagerDuty incident-created rate > alert-fired rate (ratio >1.2 indicates duplicates); track `alertmanager_notifications_total` vs `alertmanager_notifications_failed_total` delta; synthetic canary that fires one alert and asserts exactly one PagerDuty incident is created; audit log of dedup_key distribution showing any key used >1 time in <retry_window.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Notifier is here For a monitoring system watching 10,000 servers, detecting a problem is only half the job — you also have to *reach a human who can fix it*, at 3 AM, on the right team, through the right channel. The Alert Rule Engine already decides *that* something is wrong (5xx rate > 5% on payments for 10 minutes). The Notifier's job is entirely different: it's the routing and delivery layer that turns a firing alert into a phone call, a Slack message, or a Jira ticket, based on labels like `severity=page` or `team=data`. It also handles retries when PagerDuty is down, dedup so one incident doesn't page you 50 times, and silences during maintenance windows. ## What breaks without it Without a dedicated notifier, the alert engine would have to talk to PagerDuty, Slack, Jira, and email directly — and worse, it would do so *per rule evaluation*. A correlated outage (say, a bad deploy trips 200 rules at once) would fire 200 separate PagerDuty incidents for the same root cause. On-call gets a flood of pages, can't tell which matters, and meanwhile the alert engine is blocking on webhook retries instead of evaluating the next 30s tick — so *new* alerts get delayed too. ## The number that matters The design expects **~50 firing alerts on average**, but correlated incidents can push that 10–100× briefly. With 200 concurrent webhook workers and ~200ms per provider call, the notifier sustains ~1,000 deliveries/sec — enough headroom that a 5,000-alert burst drains in ~5 seconds instead of minutes. ## Trade-off The designer accepted one more moving piece (and its own failure modes) in exchange for isolating delivery concerns from alert evaluation, so a slow Slack webhook can't delay a PagerDuty page.

operations.title: Scrape + ingest a metric
operations.name: Scrape + ingest a metric
operations.description: Every 15s the collector pulls /metrics from a target, parses, and writes the samples through Kafka into the TSDB.

steps.title: Scrape tick fires — collector picks its next target batch
steps.action: At every 15s boundary the collector iterates its target list (from service discovery) and fans out HTTP GET /metrics in parallel, 100 at a time per worker.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# pseudo of the scrape loop
for tgt in discovery.list_targets(job="api"): pool.submit(scrape, tgt) def scrape(tgt): resp = http.get(f"http://{tgt.host}:{tgt.port}/metrics", timeout=10) samples = parse_exposition(resp.text) samples = attach_labels(samples, {"job": tgt.job, "instance": tgt.instance}) kafka.produce("metrics", key=series_id, value=samples)

steps.title: App renders /metrics exposition
steps.action: The Prometheus client library walks the in-process registry and writes counters, gauges, and histogram buckets to the HTTP response. Serialization is O(active series).
steps.codeOrCommand:
# exposition text returned
# HELP http_requests_total Total HTTP requests
# TYPE http_requests_total counter
http_requests_total{method="GET",status="200"} 10274
http_requests_total{method="GET",status="500"} 12
http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.1"} 9801
http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.5"} 10255
http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="+Inf"} 10286

steps.title: Collector parses and forwards to Kafka
steps.action: Collector parses the exposition text into typed samples, attaches `job` and `instance` labels, and produces one Kafka record per series keyed by series_id (hash of metric name + label set).
steps.codeOrCommand:
samples = parse_exposition(resp.text) # 1024 series, 1024 samples
for s in samples: s.labels["job"] = "api" s.labels["instance"] = "api-pod-42:9090" kafka.produce( topic="metrics", key=series_id(s), value={ "ts": now_ms, "value": s.value, "labels": s.labels } )

steps.title: Kafka durably queues the samples
steps.action: Kafka appends to the partition log with acks=all (ISR replication). Return once 2/3 brokers have fsynced the batch. Retention 4h is plenty for any downstream recovery.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# broker side
append_to_log(partition=hash(series_id) % 200, records)
wait_for_isr_ack(n=2)
acknowledge_producer

steps.title: TSDB consumer writes samples to head block + WAL
steps.action: The TSDB consumer reads from Kafka, appends each sample to the in-memory head block for its series, and mirrors the write to the write-ahead log for crash recovery. Gorilla compression happens at block compaction, not here.
steps.codeOrCommand: for rec in fetch: series = series_index.get_or_create(rec.labels) series.head.append(rec.ts, rec.value) # in-memory, ~100 ns wal.write(rec) # sequential disk, ~1 us # compaction to 2h blocks runs on its own schedule

operations.title: Query time-series (dashboard panel, last 15 min)
operations.name: Query time-series (dashboard panel, last 15 min)
operations.description: An operator opens a Grafana dashboard; Grafana issues a PromQL query for the last 15 minutes and renders a chart.

steps.title: Operator opens the API dashboard
steps.action: Browser fetches the Grafana dashboard JSON, then fires one query per panel. This flow traces a single panel: request rate per job over the last 15 minutes.
steps.codeOrCommand:
// Grafana front-end schedules panel queries in parallel
fetch(`/api/datasources/proxy/1/api/v1/query_range?query=${encodeURIComponent(q)}&start=${t0}&end=${t1}&step=15s`)

steps.title: Grafana forwards PromQL to the TSDB
steps.action: Grafana is a query proxy for this data source. It stamps the auth header and forwards the PromQL range query upstream. Variables (like `$job`) are already expanded.
steps.codeOrCommand:
GET /api/v1/query_range? query=sum(rate(http_requests_total%5B5m%5D))%20by%20(job)& start=1745520000& end=1745520900& step=15s
Authorization: Bearer <tsdb-token>

steps.title: TSDB resolves series and evaluates the range query
steps.action: The TSDB uses its inverted label index to find all series matching `http_requests_total` (say, 8 jobs × 50 instances = 400 series), streams samples from head+persistent blocks over the requested range, pipes them through the `rate(...)[5m]` operator, then `sum by (job)` reduces to 8 output series × 60 points.

steps.title: Grafana renders the chart
steps.action: Grafana receives the JSON matrix, maps each series to a legend entry, and pipes the points into the time-series panel renderer. No further aggregation server-side.
steps.codeOrCommand:
resp.data.result.forEach(s => { chart.addSeries({ name: s.metric.job, data: s.values.map(([t, v]) => [t*1000, parseFloat(v)]) })
})

steps.title: Browser draws the panel
steps.action: D3/uPlot renders the 8 lines. Total wall-clock from click to pixels: ~150–400ms including TLS and panel-layout work.

operations.title: Alert rule trigger and notify on-call
operations.name: Alert rule trigger and notify on-call
operations.description: The alert engine evaluates a PromQL rule every 30s; when 5xx rate exceeds 5% for 10 minutes, it fires and the notifier pages on-call.

steps.title: Rule evaluation tick
steps.action: Every 30s the engine iterates loaded rules and executes their PromQL expression against the TSDB. This flow follows the `HighErrorRate` rule.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# eval loop
for rule in rules: result = tsdb.query(rule.expr, at=now) rule.update_state(result, now) if rule.should_fire: notifier.emit(rule.build_alert)

steps.title: TSDB returns per-job error ratios
steps.action: The TSDB resolves both halves of the expression over the last 5m, divides elementwise, and returns only the series where the ratio > 0.05. Empty result = condition not met for any job.

steps.title: Rule stays pending — `for: 10m` not yet satisfied OR fires
steps.action: The rule has been over threshold for 6 minutes at this tick. The engine keeps state per rule: `active_since=t-6m`. Not yet 10m → alert stays `pending`. Two more evals later (12m continuous) it transitions to `firing` and emits.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# state machine per (rule, labels)
if result_non_empty and state == 'inactive': state = 'pending'; active_since = now
elif result_non_empty and state == 'pending' and now - active_since >= rule.for: state = 'firing'; emit_alert
elif result_empty: state = 'inactive'; active_since = None
steps.decision: alert threshold not crossed for `for:` duration — no notification
steps.note: This step captures the common 'pending, not yet firing' branch. On the eval where now - active_since >= 600s, state flips to `firing` and execution falls through to the notifier.

steps.title: Rule transitions to firing — emit notification
steps.action: Twelve minutes in, the state machine flips to `firing`. Engine renders annotations (with template substitution), groups by `team=payments`, and POSTs to the notifier webhook.

steps.title: Notifier routes to PagerDuty + Slack
steps.action: Notifier matches the alert's labels against its route tree. `severity=page` → PagerDuty. `team=payments` → #payments-oncall Slack. Both delivered in parallel.

steps.title: On-call's phone rings
steps.action: PagerDuty accepts the trigger, looks up the current on-call per schedule, and sends push + SMS + phone call. Total time from condition going true to the phone ringing: 10m `for:` + ≤ 30s eval granularity + ≤ 5s delivery ≈ 10m 30s.

tradeoffs.rationale: Pull makes service discovery the source of truth for 'what should exist', and a missing scrape (up == 0) is itself a first-class signal. Push hides dead targets as silent no-data.

tradeoffs.chosen: Delta-of-delta timestamps plus Gorilla XOR float compression
tradeoffs.rationale: Metric timestamps are near-regular and float values rarely change dramatically between samples; these encodings cut disk from ~16 bytes/sample to ~1.3 bytes while preserving full resolution.
Under write contention, LongAdder shards across cells to avoid the single-cache-line hot spot of AtomicLong. The extra read cost (summing cells) is paid once per scrape, not per increment.

tradeoffs.chosen: Optional push-gateway rather than extending the TSDB to accept pushes
tradeoffs.rationale: Most targets are long-lived and pull works beautifully; a narrow push-gateway for cron-style jobs keeps the main path simple without forcing the whole system into push semantics.

tradeoffs.chosen: Remote-write to Thanos/Mimir/VictoriaMetrics instead of scaling local TSDB
tradeoffs.rationale: Local TSDB is optimised for recent data and a single host; multi-month retention and global query need a horizontally scalable store. Remote-write decouples ingest from long-term storage evolution.

tradeoffs.chosen: Fixed bucket boundaries rather than sparse/exponential histograms
tradeoffs.rationale: Fixed buckets are trivial to aggregate across instances and simple to reason about in PromQL; the loss of precision at the tails is worth the operational simplicity at fleet scale.
